item.title: Can Getting Naked With Strangers Improve Body Image?
item.description:
Body Image

Can Getting Naked With Strangers Improve Body Image?

What I learned from a weekend away getting nude with strangers.

Posted August 15, 2026

Key points
  • Cultural attitudes toward nudity are learned, not innate.
  • Shifting how we relate to our own nakedness can be a meaningful step in healing.
  • Non-sexual nude spaces are linked in research to greater self-esteem and life satisfaction.
Source: Emiliano Vittoriosi/Pexels

"No, you can't take your shirt off," they say, as the boys frolic naked through the sprinklers and my own shirt hangs heavy and wrong.

“She’s put on a bit of weight hasn’t she” the family discusses as I play in earshot, desperately wishing I could disappear.

“I want to split her in two” one of the footy boys tells my friend on my first day at high school, as I desperately try and figure out what that means.

“wolf whistle” “show us your tits” “begging for it hey” they scream, whilst I look straight ahead and pretend not to hear.

I was a child for each of these moments. My body has been public property for as long as I can remember.

If the statements sound generic, like you’ve heard them before, it’s probably because you have. This kind of commentary on female bodies is so normal that most of us don't flinch anymore. I certainly stopped.

Somewhere along the way I grew comfortable with the idea that my body was on display at all times. That unless I was completely alone, there was almost nowhere I wouldn’t be looked at and judged. My body was never simply just a body. Even my nakedness meant something. It was rarely allowed to be simply a state.

What the Research Says

Like all good scientists, I started to question these ideas and the story I was telling myself. And after more than a decade studying and practising psychology and sexology, I can finally say I’ve started telling myself a new one.

Let’s cut back to the first time I really challenged these ideas about my naked body. I was in Japan and had headed off to indulge in one of the onsens. It had views of snowy mountains; how could I say no? This was my first taste of being naked among others in a communal setting, and the strangest thing happened. My body was just another body. No stares, no commentary, and no judgement that I could detect. In fact, I felt a sense of community, being shown what to do so I could belong. This was a far cry away from always feeling on display.

And the science is with me on this discovery, that our attitudes toward nudity are culturally shaped, not universal (West, 2018). What I'd spent my life treating as the natural order was actually just one culture's version of it. Take Germany, for example, and their Freikörperkultur (FKK) Tradition. The FKK ("Free Body Culture") movement, which dates back more than a century, treats nudity as connected to health and recreation rather than sexuality (Wagner, 2005). Spaces like parks, beaches, lakes, and spas include designated nude spaces that are socially acceptable. We see this in other communities and cultures too, where nudity is understood as an ordinary state, not a statement.

article continues after advertisement

And it goes even deeper than that. Studies have linked participation in these contexts to greater body appreciation, reduced body shame, and higher life satisfaction (West, 2020). My personal experience has mirrored this. After the onsens, I started seeking the same experiences back home in Australia. Places where my nudity could be ordinary outside of a sexual context. Nude beaches, nude yoga, creating a nude home, the list goes on. A far cry from my youth, where everything about my body was monitored, sexualised, and judged. There was a sense of safety and connection in the shared agreement of these spaces. And as corny as it sounds, it has been these spaces which have made me feel at home in my body.

What I Learned From a Weekend of Nude Strangers

Cut to the beginning of this year, when I signed up for a weekend away with nine other women, strangers to me at the time, to be nude in shared spaces. We sunbathed, jumped from boats, shared meals, took baths, swam in the ocean, and allowed our bodies to simply be. At one point, one lady looked at another lady, exclaiming, “We have the same tattoo,” a small tattoo on each of their breasts that had until that moment been overlooked. Because no one was on show. Our nudity was not being monitored, sexualised, or judged. And that type of freedom and acceptance changes how you see and live in your body. It has been what has allowed me to rewrite my own story that had been shaped by fear so long ago.

If you've read this far and something in you ached or wanted to argue, that's worth paying attention to. It's usually a sign of how deep this stuff runs. In my work with clients navigating body shame and the messier parts of intimacy, this is often where the real change starts. We are not fixing the body, but instead questioning what we were taught it means to be seen. Full disclaimer: You don't need a weekend away with strangers to do that! It's starting small and curiously, because if your body has never just been allowed to be a body, maybe it's time it was.
